title: TC1-20893
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), and her minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Oldest Child) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Youngest Child) (collectively, Appellants) appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), and her minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Oldest Child) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Youngest Child) (collectively, Appellants) appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection. The Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child are citizens of Nigeria while the Youngest Child is a citizen of the United States of America (USA). The Principal Appellant was the designated representative for the Oldest Child, and an Independent Designated Representative was appointed for the Youngest Child.

The Appellants allege fear of harmful rituals at the hands of the Principal Appellant's extended family members if they were to return to Nigeria. In a November 18, 2021 RPD Decision, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claim, finding that the fear of the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child is not well-founded, and that they therefore do not have a serious possibility of persecution as required by section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).2 Further, the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child have failed to establish that they would be personally subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk of danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment upon return to Nigeria. Lastly, the RPD found that the Youngest Child is not a Convention3 refugee or a person in need of protection as, notwithstanding issues of family separation, he can return safely to the USA.4

On appeal, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to consider the compelling reasons for granting the Principal Appellant protection based on her previous persecution, pursuant to section 108(4) of the IRPA,5 and erred in concluding that there is not more than a mere possibility that the Principal Appellant's extended family would take the Oldest Child by force.6

I disagree with the Appellants. I find that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, and have failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they would personally be subjected to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to Nigeria.
The appeal is dismissed, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.7 The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The following is a summary of the Appellants' allegations contained in their Basis of Claim (BOC) form narratives and oral testimonies at the RPD Hearing.

The Appellants allege fear of harmful rituals at the hands of the Principal Appellant's extended family members if they were to return to Nigeria. The Principal Appellant's father was a local XXXX in Nigeria, and at the time of his death in XXXX 2014, the Principal Appellant was pregnant with the Oldest Child. During the nine-day period of mourning, and as a result of her pregnancy, the extended family subjected the Principal Appellant to inhumane rituals. More specifically, they locked her in a room naked, made incisions on her body, and made her drink concoctions of blood. After the birth of the Oldest Child, he was expected to undergo additional rituals, including painful incisions. As a result, the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child fled first to other cities in Nigeria, and eventually to the USA, where she gave birth to the Youngest Child, before eventually coming to Canada.

Section 110(4) of the IRPA8 provides that appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. Where the new evidence meets one of the legislative factors in section 110(4), the next step of the analysis is for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh9 and assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance, and newness.

The Appellants submit a letter from the Principal Appellant's sister dated XXXX XXXX, 2021, which is accompanied by a photocopy of her passport and photographs of the 2021 Christmas celebration (Sister's Letter).10

I find that the Sister's Letter meets one of the legislative factors set out in section 110(4) of the IRPA. This document is new as it post-dates the RPD Decision and pertains to events that occurred after the rejection of the claim. Further, I find that this document meets the criteria set out in Singh and Raza. This new document appears credible on its face, and I have no reason to doubt the source and circumstances in which it came about. They are relevant in that it pertains to the ongoing interest of the Principal Appellant's extended family members to subject the Oldest Child to the rituals. The Appellants submit that during their family's 2021 Christmas celebration, two high priests came looking for the Oldest Child with the intention of subjecting him to the rituals. The Chief Priest threatened that they would "stop at nothing" to accomplish this.11 For the above reasons, I admit the Sister's Letter as new evidence.

The Appellants do not request an oral hearing. Under section 110(6) of the IRPA,12 the RAD may hold a hearing if there is new evidence that raises a serious issue with respect to the appellant's credibility, which is central to the decision in the claim and, if accepted, would justify accepting or rejecting the claim. In this case, I find that the new evidence does not meet the criteria to hold a hearing. I further find that there is sufficient evidence on record to arrive at a decision. Accordingly, it is not necessary for me to hold a hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.13

I have conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence, including the Appellant's Record in its entirety and the oral testimonies at the RPD Hearing. I have also considered and applied Chairperson's Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.14

I acknowledge all the Appellants' arguments. However, I will address only those arguments that are determinative of the outcome of the appeal. Exclusion The Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child do not have Permanent Residence Status in the USA

The RPD found that the Appellants have established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child do not have legal permanent residence status in the USA, and that they neither had such status in the past and lost it, nor had access to such status and failed to seek it. The Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child are, accordingly, not excluded by Section E of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention.15 In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I agree with and confirm the RPD's finding for the same reasons provided by the RPD. The Principal Appellant is not excluded pursuant to Section F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention

The RPD found that the Appellants have established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Principal Appellant's American husband does not have any parental rights to the Youngest Child, and that therefore the Principal Appellant has proper consent for both of her children to accompany her to, and remain in, Canada. Accordingly, the RPD found that there are no serious reasons for considering that the Principal Appellant has committed a serious non-political crime, and she is therefore not excluded by Section F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention.16 In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I agree with and confirm the RPD's finding for the same reasons provided by the RPD. Nexus

I note that the RPD did not clearly identify the nexus to a Convention ground, but nonetheless assessed whether there was a serious possibility of persecution. I do not find this to be a determinative error. Moreover, as I will explain below, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child have not established a serious possibility of persecution. For the same reasons, I also find that the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child have not established a section 97(1)17 risk, on a balance of probabilities, which has a higher standard of proof than a claim under section 96. The Appellants and their allegations are generally credible

The RPD stated that for the purposes of the RPD Decision, it has not drawn any negative credibility inference against the Appellants except with regard to the ability of their extended family to use spiritual powers to compel participation in the rituals, which the RPD did not accept.18 I agree.

I have reviewed the Appellants' Record in its entirety, including the audio recording of the hearing. I find that the Appellants are generally credible witnesses. I further find that the Appellants were honestly endeavouring to tell the truth at the RPD Hearing and their testimonies were direct, spontaneous, and detailed. I do not find that there were any material contradictions, inconsistencies or omissions between the Appellants' BOC, their testimonies and the documentary evidence that were not reasonably explained by them. I also do not find that there were sufficient credibility issues to rebut the presumption that the Appellants' sworn testimonies are true.19 The Appellants' allegations are further corroborated by the documentary evidence on record. Accordingly, I find that the Appellants and their allegations are generally credible. However, I agree with the RPD in drawing a negative credibility inference against the Appellants with regard to the ability of their extended family to use spiritual powers to compel participation in the rituals, which I will discuss below. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants had not established a well-founded fear of persecution The Youngest Child can return safely to the USA

The Principal Appellant testified that the Youngest Child did not fear anything in the USA, and that no one in the USA was trying to harm him. As such, the RPD found that the Youngest Child is not a Convention Refugee or a person in need of protection as, notwithstanding issues of family separation, the Youngest Child can return safely to the USA.20 The Appellants do not contest this finding. In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I agree with and confirm the RPD's finding for the same reasons provided by the RPD. The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellants have failed to establish more than a mere possibility that the Principal Appellant or the Oldest Child will be forced to participate in these rituals Physical Force

The Appellants submit that the RPD improperly assessed the risk that the Principal Appellant's relatives would physically force the Oldest Child into the rituals and therefore erred by finding that there was not more than a mere possibility of persecution. Further, the Appellants submit that the fact that their relatives could commit such atrocious acts against a pregnant family member should be sufficient to establish a reasonable possibility that they would physically force another party to undergo the same rituals. Lastly, the Appellants submitted new evidence that the high priests have been looking for the Oldest Child as recently as XXXX 2021, which suggests that they are highly motivated to conduct the rituals. Their persistence, along with the appalling nature of the rituals, establishes that the Principal Appellant's family members are extremists who present at least a reasonable possibility of persecution against the Oldest Child.21 I disagree.

In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I agree with the RPD's finding that the Appellants have not established more than a mere possibility that the Principal Appellant's extended family would use physical force to make the Older Child undergo rituals to which the Principal Appellant objects.22

As noted by the RPD in the RPD Decision, the Principal Appellant testified that if she was near her extended family, they could possibly physically take the Oldest Child from her to conduct the rituals, but that she has never seen them take anyone's child, they have never threatened physical force to take the Oldest Child to perform the rituals, and that she does not know if they would use physical force.23 The RPD also noted the Principal Appellant's testimony that when she attempted to refuse the rituals they imposed upon her, her extended family told her she had to undergo them, and that if she had further refused, she could have been pushed into them. However, she also testified that she had never seen anyone be physically forced into participating in the rituals which she underwent and that she was merely speculating as to the possibility.24 The Principal Appellant further testified that her extended family told her she had to come to the one-year anniversary of her father's death in an attempt to force the Oldest Child to participate in the rituals, but that she was able to refuse that without being forced to attend.25

Moreover, the RPD noted that the Appellants submitted no further evidence suggesting any physical force would be used to make the Oldest Child undergo the rituals to which the Principal Appellant objects. In particular, the RPD stated that the documentary disclosure provided by the Appellants makes no reference to any physical force threatened by the extended family to compel participation in the rituals by the Oldest Child and makes no reference to any prior use of physical force in similar situations.26

I acknowledge the Appellants' submission that when asked if she has any evidence that her family would forcefully take her son, the Principal Appellant testified that "they normally say that if I don't provide my son, they will take him and do whatever they want to do."27 I also acknowledge the Appellants' submission that the Principal Appellant's sister stated in the Sister's Letter that the Chief Priest said they would "stop at nothing."28 I further acknowledge the Appellants' submission that the RPD relied heavily on the fact that the Principal Appellant had never witnessed her relatives physically force anyone to undergo the rituals as this was the first royal succession ceremony in the Principal Appellant's lifetime.29 However, having considered the evidence that the Principal Appellant's extended family has not threatened or used physical force to make the Older Child undergo the rituals to which the Principal Appellant objects, I agree with the RPD's finding that the evidence does not establish more than a mere possibility that the extended family would use physical force to make the Oldest Child undergo the rituals. Spiritual Force

As noted by the RPD in the RPD Decision, the Principal Appellant testified that her extended family could force the rituals on the Oldest Child by using a spiritual force to compel the rituals and/or harm the Oldest Child. The Principal Appellant also testified that the Oldest Child could be harmed physically, but she explained that this was through the spiritual force that her family could use.30

The RPD found that the use of spiritual powers to compel the involuntary participation in rituals is one of the clearest of cases where it is outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected. Further, the RPD found that it is implausible that the Principal Appellant's extended family could use spiritual powers to compel the participation of the Oldest Child in rituals to which the Principal Appellant objects, or to otherwise harm the Oldest Child.31

Moreover, the RPD considered the objective evidence indicating that a parent can obtain police protection if they have family members who want to apply tribal markings to their child, and that the practice of scarification varies depending on where one resides.32 Accordingly, the RPD found that the objective evidence fails to establish more than a mere possibility that the Oldest Child will be forced to undergo such a ritual.33

The Appellants do not contest the RPD's findings. In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I agree with and confirm the RPD's findings in this regard for the same reasons provided by the RPD.

Additionally, the RPD noted that the Appellants did not testify to any other ways that their extended family would force the Oldest Child to participate in the rituals.34 The Principal Appellant also testified that there are no further rituals to which her extended family seek to perform against her.35

In my independent assessment, and having considered the evidence, I find that the RPD did not err in finding that the Appellants have failed to establish more than a mere possibility that the Principal Appellant or the Oldest Child will be forced to participate in these rituals. Accordingly, I further find that the RPD did not err in finding that the fear of the Principal Appellant and the Oldest Child is not well-founded, and that they therefore do not have a serious possibility of persecution as required by section 96 of the IRPA.36

Additionally, I find that the RPD did not err in finding that as section 97 of the IRPA requires a higher probability of risk than section 96, the Principal Appellant's and the Oldest Child's failure to establish more than a mere possibility of harm in Nigeria necessarily means they have failed to establish that they would be personally subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk of danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment upon return to Nigeria. Furthermore, I note that section 97(1)(a) was not raised before the RPD, and I concur with the RPD that there is nothing in the evidence to suggest that the Appellants would face a danger of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture.37 Section 108(4) of the IRPA is not applicable in this case

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to consider that the Principal Appellant's past persecution, specifically, her experience of the rituals which were appalling and atrocious, constitutes compelling reasons for her not to be returned to Nigeria.38 Further, the Appellants submit that the RPD made an implicit finding that the Principal Appellant's past persecution meets the "compelling reasons" threshold under either of the two standards discussed in the case law.39 The Appellants explained that the first approach considers whether the past persecution was "appalling" or "atrocious" while the second approach considers all of the circumstances of the case, including the Appellants' age, cultural background, previous social experiences, and the trauma caused by repatriation.40 Lastly, the Appellants provided a letter from a Nurse Practitioner confirming that the Principal Appellant meets the criteria for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which is a significant consideration in a "compelling reasons" analysis, specifically, as it relates to the potential for re-traumatization caused by repatriation.41 I am not persuaded by the Appellants' arguments.

The RPD did not make a finding with respect to section 108(4) of the IRPA, nor did the Appellants raise this argument before the RPD. For the following reasons, I find that the RPD was correct in not assessing section 108(4) of the IRPA because the Appellants did not establish that the reasons for which they sought protection have ceased to exist, which is a precondition for the application of section 108(4).

The jurisprudence is clear that the RPD should not undertake a section 108(4) assessment in every case. The Federal Court of Appeal in Yamba concluded that there is an obligation to consider whether there are compelling reasons "in every case in which the Refugee Division concludes that a claimant has suffered past persecution, but [there] has been a change of country conditions."42

Moreover, the Federal Court stated the following in Contreras Martinez: [19] ...It is only when para. 108(1)(e) is invoked by the RPD that a "compelling reasons" assessment should be made, i.e. when the refugee claimant was found to be a refugee but nevertheless had been be denied refugee status given the change of circumstances in the country of origin. In Kalumba c. Canada (Ministre de la Citoyenneté et de l'Immigration), 2005 CF 680, [2005] A.C.F. No. 879, at para. 18 and 19, Justice Shore provided a succinct summary of the applicable principles: [MY TRANSLATION] As per the wording of the section, before considering the application of subsection 108(4) of the Act, the Commission must conclude that the person would have been granted refugee status notwithstanding the change of circumstances which occurred in the country. In the matter at hand, the Commission determined that M. Kalumba had an internal flight alternative in his country of origin and therefore concluded that Mr. Kalumba was neither a refugee nor a person in need of protection as per sections 96 and 97 of the Act. Secondly, the Commission never mentions in its reasons such a change of circumstances in the RC that would have an effect of depriving the grounds for his fear of persecution. As such, the Commission did not have to conduct a "compelling reasons" analysis pursuant to subsection 108(4) of the Act. ... [21] It is clear from the wording of sub. 108(4) that it is not aimed at creating a broad obligation for the RPD to assess the existence of "compelling reasons" in every refugee claim. If a refugee claimant is neither a refugee nor a person in need of protection because the conditions of the general definition of section 96 and 97 of the IRPA are not met, then no "compelling reasons" assessment need be performed by the RPD. It is only necessary where the rejection of the claim is based on 108(1)(e).43

According to the relevant jurisprudence, before the Immigration and Refugee Board can consider whether there are sufficient compelling reasons to grant refugee status under section 108(4), the Appellants must not only establish that at some point they met the definition of a Convention refugee or a protected person, but that it must be determined that the reasons for the claim have ceased to exist due to country conditions.44 In this case, the RPD has not invoked paragraph 108(1)(e)45 in rejecting the Appellants' claim based on a change of circumstances. The Appellants have not argued that there has been a change of circumstances in Nigeria that would have the effect of depriving the grounds for their fear of persecution46 or that would result in a claim for refugee protection no longer being available.47 The Appellants do not argue, nor has there been any finding, that their risk at the hands of the Principal Appellant's extended family members has ceased to exist. On the contrary, the Appellants have submitted new evidence that the high priests have been looking for the Oldest Child as recently as XXXX 2021, seven years after the XXXX death.48 Absent a change of circumstances in this case as contemplated in section 108(4) and the relevant jurisprudence, I find that section 108(4) is not applicable.

In my independent assessment, and having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, and have failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they would personally be subjected to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to Nigeria.

The appeal is dismissed. I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
